title: Sector Skills Development Program
text:
Official
Electricity Supply Industry Graduate Skills Development Program
SUMMARY CONCEPT NOTE
1. Background
The Electricity Supply Industry (ESI) is a knowledge-intensive sector that depends on a
highly skilled workforce to ensure safe, reliable, and efficient operations. Historically,
these capabilities were cultivated through structured industrial training for fresh
graduates and through continuous professional development for industry personnel.
This emphasis on skills development began as early as 1954 with the commissioning of
Uganda's first electricity generation facility and the establishment of the Njeru Training
School. Under the vertically integrated Uganda Electricity Board (UEB), the Njeru
school became a central pillar in producing technically competent engineers and
technicians who sustained the sector for decades.
However, the sector reforms that unbundled UEB in 2001 significantly disrupted this
once-coherent training ecosystem. While the reforms improved operational efficiency
by creating specialized entities for generation, transmission, distribution, and
regulation, they also dismantled the centralized training mechanism that had
historically nurtured industry-ready professionals. In the absence of a unified training
pipeline, each licensee developed its own internal training approach, resulting in
fragmented, inconsistent, and often insufficient preparation for new entrants to this
specialized, high-risk technical environment.
This fragmentation, coupled with a shrinking workforce due to the retirement of UEB-
era professionals, has become increasingly consequential as Uganda's ESI expands to
meet the demands of Vision 2040 and successive National Development Plans. The
sector now requires specialized technical and supervisory competencies, yet many
graduates enter the workforce with strong theoretical backgrounds but limited
practical exposure. This mismatch has contributed to prolonged learning curves and
uneven professional development across institutions. Left unaddressed, these gaps
threaten the operational excellence and the long-term sustainability of Uganda's
power sector.
Recognizing the urgency of these challenges, the Electricity Regulatory Authority
(ERA) in 2016 initiated efforts to revive structured sector-wide skills development. This
led to the establishment of the Graduate Skills Development Program (GSDP),
designed to rebuild a consistent pipeline of industry-ready graduates by providing
practical exposure, mentorship, and standardized training across the ESI. The
1

Official
Graduate Skills Development Program implemented by the Licensees became
effective 1st January 2017.
2. Contextual Analysis
After the unbundling of UEB and prior to the commencement of the sector skills
development program, Uganda’s electricity subsector lacked a structured,
harmonized mechanism for skills development and for transitioning fresh entrants from
academic learning to professional competence within the Electricity Supply Industry
(ESI). Capacity-building practices across licensees remained highly variable, with
entities relying on fragmented, internally driven training models that do not
consistently equip new graduates with the technical exposure and supervisory
support required in such a demanding and a high-risk industry. Such an inconsistency
results in an uneven workforce pipeline, one marked by skill gaps, prolonged learning
curves, and limited alignment between academic preparation and sectoral
demands. Compounding this challenge, the subsector continues to experience
internal mobility and turnover as professionals move between entities without the
parallel development of new talent to replenish the system. A coordinated graduate
development framework is therefore critical to stabilizing the talent pipeline,
improving sector-wide capability, and supporting the long-term modernization and
reliability of Uganda’s electricity infrastructure.
3. Goal and Objectives of the GSDP
The overall goal of the Graduate Skills Development Program (GSDP) is to transform
university graduates into competent, industry-ready professionals through structured
learning experiences across the Electricity Supply Industry (ESI). The program was
conceptualized as a bridge between academic preparation and professional
practice, ensuring that graduates acquire the practical skills, sector ethos, and
professional values required for effective performance in a high-risk technical
environment. Through rotational placements, hands-on coaching, mentorship, and
project-based assignments, the GSDP equips trainees with the technical
competence, safety consciousness, and leadership potential needed to contribute
meaningfully to Uganda’s evolving power sector.
Specifically, the GSDP aims to:
a) Bridge the gap between classroom learning and the demands of real-world
technical practice.
b) Provide consistent, structured exposure to operations within generation,
transmission, and distribution.
c) Strengthen safety culture, mentorship quality, and professional conduct across
the sector.
d) Build a sustainable pipeline of skilled professionals to support long-term sector
reliability, modernization, and workforce renewal.
4. Training Duration
The GSDP is a three-year program that targets recent graduates across various
professional fields that form the core and support frameworks of ESI operations. During
implementation, trainees are expected to be rotated through key operational
2

Official
environments, including power plants, substations, distribution networks, and system
control centers. Each rotation is meant to involve supervised practical work, structured
mentorship, and periodic assessments.
The program integrates professional development with soft skills, including leadership,
problem-solving, ethics, and technical reporting, to cultivate well-rounded industry
professionals. By the end of a cohort, every trainee will have acquired hands-on
experience, enhanced analytical capabilities, and a strong grounding in sector norms
and expectations.
5. Implementation Strategy
The implementation of the Graduate Skills Development Program (GSDP) follows a
coordinated model between the Electricity Regulatory Authority (ERA) and licensed
electricity sector entities. ERA provides strategic oversight and financing through
annual budget approvals, policy direction, and implementation guidelines, ensuring
that the program remains aligned with national workforce priorities. Licensees are
responsible for operationalizing the program by competitively recruiting graduate
trainees, delivering structured rotational training, and submitting annual performance
reports to ERA. As part of the approval process, ERA requires each licensee to develop
a comprehensive three-year training plan detailing the knowledge-transfer themes,
technical competencies, and field-based learning activities relevant to the
professions being recruited, including engineering, economics, and finance.
To maintain quality and accountability, ERA conducts an annual program review to
assess progress, document outcomes, and identify areas for continuous improvement.
The program also incorporates mandatory composition standards to promote gender
inclusion and professional balance: a minimum gender ratio of 60:40 (male to female)
and an engineering-to-other-disciplines ratio of 70:30. Participating licensees are
further required to submit detailed accountability and performance reports for the
allocated funds no later than 28 February of the following year. These measures ensure
transparency, strengthen program effectiveness, and reinforce the GSDP as a
sustainable pipeline for developing industry-ready professionals within Uganda’s
electricity supply industry.
6. Outcomes
The Graduate Skills Development Program is expected to produce a steady stream of
technically competent professionals for Uganda’s electricity sector while
strengthening sector coherence through shared training standards and expectations.
By equipping graduates with practical skills, sector-specific values, and a strong safety
culture, the program aims to improve operational performance and system reliability
across the ESI. In a context where the electricity sector faces growing competition
and poaching of skilled staff by the oil and gas industry alongside an aging workforce,
the GSDP provides a vital pipeline of new talent, including emerging opportunities in
the rapidly expanding renewable energy subsector.
The program also helps bridge persistent skills mismatches between industry needs
and current academic preparation, enhancing the sector's attractiveness to young
professionals, increasing retention, and rebuilding institutional memory weakened by

past reforms. Ultimately, the GSDP is designed to reduce reliance on ad hoc in-house
training and to contribute to Uganda’s long-term economic transformation by
developing a skilled, future-ready energy workforce.
7. Conclusion
The proposed GSDP addresses a critical gap in Uganda’s electricity sector by
introducing a structured, collaborative, and future-oriented approach to human-
capital development. It offers a strategic pathway for equipping young professionals
with the skills, values, and competencies required to sustain and modernize the ESI.
Establishing this program in 2017 meant the sector had secured a long-term pipeline
of technical capacity that contributed meaningfully to national development.
